position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a 406 MHz distress beacon targeted at outdoor recreation enthusiasts. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey to validate the market demand and refine the proposition. Based on the survey results, decide whether to proceed with product development and marketing.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: While technology effectiveness remains important, other factors such as ease of use, distribution channels, and brand reputation also play a significant role in the adoption of 406 MHz distress beacons by outdoor recreation enthusiasts.
T1.who_benefits: Individual hikers, campers, and outdoor adventurers who need a lightweight, automatic distress signal device.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on unreliable or cumbersome methods; a distress beacon that works with existing satellite networks and can be deployed without additional training would reduce risk and increase confidence in remote activities.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through registration fees, and build brand awareness among outdoor communities.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. were stable or growing in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety features that reduce risk.
Distribution channels (e.g., outdoor retailers) exist for direct-to-consumer sales.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation groups would show >60% would consider purchasing a 406 MHz distress beacon.
Sales of the device would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation density (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges).
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon because it provides a reliable, long-range emergency communication solution that is easier to use than existing methods (e.g., satellite phones, radio).

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search-and-rescue teams will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, reliable signal that can be detected across vast geographic areas, reducing response time and cost.
T2.who_benefits: Search-and-rescue agencies, coast guards, and emergency management organizations that need to locate and assist remote individuals quickly.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Current methods often rely on multiple frequencies and inconsistent signal strengths; a standardized 406 MHz beacon would simplify detection and coordination, leading to faster response and potentially saving lives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the device to government agencies and NGOs at volume prices, secure long-term contracts for service contracts (e.g., registration, data transmission), and gain credibility as a reliable emergency solution.
assumptions: Government agencies budget for emergency communication upgrades in 2002.
Standardization reduces procurement costs and training requirements.
Existing SAR teams are willing to adopt new technology if it demonstrably improves efficiency.
predictions: A survey of SAR agencies would show >50% would consider purchasing 406 MHz beacons for operational use.
Sales would be concentrated in regions with high SAR activity (e.g., coastlines, mountain ranges).

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation Distress Beacon
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown a description of a 406 MHz distress beacon (specifying outdoor recreation use case) and asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (Yes/No). Additional questions: (1) What is the maximum price you would pay? (2) Which benefit matters most to you: reliable long-range distress signal (T1) or standardized signal for SAR teams (T2).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults who have participated in outdoor recreation activities in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by age (18-35, 36-55, 55+), gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: benefit preference (reliable distress signal vs standardized SAR signal).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 45% of participants will indicate purchase intent and a maximum price of at least €250.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will indicate purchase intent and a maximum price of at least €250, but the majority will cite the benefit of standardized SAR signal.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent ≥45% AND average maximum price ≥€250, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If purchase intent <40% OR average maximum price <€200, conclude there is insufficient demand to justify investment.

revisions.reason: New evidence from a simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) shows that a different type of technology (label printer) had a minor impact on packing errors, indicating that the effectiveness of a distress beacon's technology in improving safety is not the only factor that influences consumer adoption. This evidence weakens the claim that 406 MHz distress beacons will be widely adopted by outdoor recreation enthusiasts based
revisions.new_claim: While technology effectiveness remains important, other factors such as ease of use, distribution channels, and brand reputation also play a significant role in the adoption of 406 MHz distress beacons by outdoor recreation enthusiasts.

arguments.measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: benefit preference (reliable distress signal vs standardized SAR signal).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 45% of participants will indicate purchase intent and a maximum price of at least €250.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will indicate purchase intent and a maximum price of at least €250, but the majority will cite the benefit of standardized SAR signal.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent ≥45% AND average maximum price ≥€250, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If purchase intent <40% OR average maximum price <€200, conclude there is insufficient demand to justify investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a tool that can handle various chores; the tractor's low price and ease of use make it attractive compared to manual tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding the need for new retail channels.

Consumers trust Deere's brand for agricultural equipment and will extend that trust to lawn and garden products.

T1.claim: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and easy to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking affordable, versatile garden tools; Deere benefits by selling tractors directly or through dealers, capturing higher margins than bulk farm equipment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly rising sales of garden tractors (76% growth 1960-1979) indicates homeowners shift from manual tools to powered equipment; the low cost and multi-use capability make the shift attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price tractors modestly and sell accessories, earning revenue from a new consumer segment while leveraging existing tractor engineering.
assumptions: Small-garden homeowners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a tractor.
They value time-saving and multi-use functionality.
Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a price point comparable to early 1960s consumer goods for a garden tractor.
Pilot sales of a basic garden tractor will exceed dealer expectations within 12 weeks.
Accessory sales (e.g., mower blades, snow blowers) will be higher than for farm tractors.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: The rise of suburban home ownership and the desire for neat yards create a market for convenient yard tools; the low price point makes the tractor accessible for occasional use, shifting from manual to powered tools.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell a basic tractor at a modest price and bundle accessories, generating revenue from a new segment while leveraging existing tractor technology.

Deere can reach this segment through existing dealer network or new direct channels.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to purchase a tractor priced at a level comparable to 1960s consumer goods for occasional yard work.
